subject: history
title: The 1973 Oil Shock: One Cut, One Price Jump
objectives: Explain why the October 1973 OPEC embargo made the world oil price jump from about $3 to about $12 a barrel
Trace the stage-by-stage pass-on of the oil price rise into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices
Explain why households cut spending back at the end of the chain

definitions.meaning: The October 1973 ban by OPEC on oil exports to selected importing countries: the cut that closes the valve on the supply flow in the animation.
The price of a barrel of crude oil on the world market: about $3 a barrel before the shock and about $12 a barrel after the jump.
A sudden cut in the supply of a key input that pushes its price up from the supply side, as the embargo did to oil in 1973.
The cost of what goes into making or moving a product: oil and transport are input costs for almost everything.
Each stage charging its higher costs to the next: dearer oil into transport costs, transport into factory costs, factory costs into shop prices.
What households buy at the prices they face: it falls back at the end of the chain as households cut spending in response to higher prices.

mechanismSteps: Before the shock: oil flows freely at about $3 a barrel - crude oil moves steadily from OPEC oil fields to importing countries along one supply route, and the world price sits at about $3 a barrel (s1).
October 1973: the embargo closes the valve on the flow - OPEC embargoes exports, no oil crosses the closed valve, and the world price jumps from about $3 to about $12 a barrel (s2).
Stage by stage: dearer oil becomes dearer everything - transport costs rise first, factory costs rise next, and shop prices rise last as each stage passes the one rise on (s3).
Spending falls back: households buy less - faced with higher prices, households cut spending back, the demand bar falls, and importing economies slow (s4).
workedExample: Work through the whole chain for the 1973 shock. Step 1 (s1): before the shock the world oil price is about $3 a barrel and oil flows without interruption. Step 2 (s2): the embargo cuts the flow, so the price jumps from about $3 to about $12 a barrel - a rise of about $9, roughly four times the old price. Step 3 (s3): because oil and transport are inputs to almost everything, the rise is passed on stage by stage into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices, in that order. Step 4 (s4): households cut spending back, so demand falls while prices stay high - one cut, one jump, a chain of higher prices, then less spending.

trap.misconception: The 1973 oil crisis pushed prices up because governments printed extra money to pay for dearer oil.
trap.explanation: The slip: Prices did rise across the economy after 1973, and governments do print money - so it is easy to read the general inflation as money-printing that happened to coincide with dearer oil. The fix: The price rises started on the supply side, not the money side: the OPEC embargo cut the flow of oil, the world oil price jumped from about $3 to about $12 a barrel, and because oil and transport are inputs to almost everything, that one rise was passed on stage by stage into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices while households cut spending back. In class, replay scene 2: freeze at the closed valve and ask what has changed at that exact moment - the flow of oil, not the money supply - then run scene 3 to watch the one rise reach transport costs, factory costs and shop prices.
